payload.body:
> I would be happy to drop this test to be honest, it was Claude-coded and had to be assembly in order to bypass the confluence of factors that expose this bug: optimizations (specialisations + inlining), and code layout.

It's only swapping one bag of inscrutable bytes for a different one, but I added a tool last year specifically for this kind of test case:  yaml2macho-core.  Look at the test case in `lldb/test/API/functionalities/unwind/cortex-m-exception` for an example of how it's used.  You create an objectfile.json with the address ranges & names of a few functions.  You create a .yaml file with some register values for some threads, and then you supply stack memory and the text instructions of the functions you're backtracing through (so lldb can do an instruction emulation of them and create an UnwindPlan).

There's no way to package eh_frame/dwarf_frame unwind instructions in the tests today - it's only useful when instruction emulation or the default unwind plans are sufficient to repo the issue.  But it makes it very simple to take a proprietary or large firmware/kernel repo case and extract just the stack memory needed to reproduce an unwind issue.

Another example arm64 unwind test case is in `lldb/test/API/functionalities/unwind/outlined-functions`.  I've written a few different API tests using the tool, it's really quick to assemble the necessary information in a .yaml file.

One problem I had with hand-written assembly repo cases in the past is that the assembly syntax needed for Mach-O was different than ELF, and I ended up writing tests that required they be run on one or the other systems.  Having lldb create a corefile from specifications removes the runtime details.

payload.author: rapidsna
payload.body:
> @rapidsna do you think the AttributedType ought to be applied right at the PointerType, or outermost? I imagine long term we'll want it outersmost, but not sure if we want to minimise the impedance mismatch to begin with.

Good question! I don't think it's necessarily right at the pointer type, and not necessarily outermost either. That depends on whether other attributes are written later in the source. In particular, any late-parsed attribute would end up outermost relative to others (in theory, assuming they can co-exist).

Also worth noting, related to the co-existing point: I don't think we necessarily allow single and counted_by to be written together anymore in this approach, though I suspect there's existing code that relies on it.

payload.author: benlangmuir
payload.body:
> I don't know how do we use ASTUnit? Does it have a long life time in indexer?

We use ASTUnit for editor features like code-completion, looking up symbol for the cursor position, etc. and generally that will keep the ASTUnit around as long as the file is still active in the editor, with something like a small LRU cache so you don't have too many open at once. The compiler instance itself gets dropped after parsing finishes, but we keep the Sema, ASTContext, ASTReader, etc. inside the ASTUnit.

So the possible concern would be you might keep the CAS open as long as any open file in the IDE made use of it.  I'm not sure if we should be worried about this or not.

payload.author: delcypher
payload.body:
Because this is so large I had claude look over the changes and look for dropped/added bounds checks and changes to the conditions used on `br` instructions leading to checks. Looks mostly good. Claude said

---

1. Added/removed llvm.ubsantrap — CLEAN. Exactly 5 removed / 5 added, all paired, all @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 25). The only change is the !annotation match format (!{{[0-9]+}} / {{!annotation ...}} → named [[META]]).
  unreachable also balances 5/5; soft-trap @trap.reason strings balance 27/27 (content identical, only align 4→align 1).

  2. Branch conditions to trap blocks — CLEAN (one safe addition). Only 3 of 137 files touch any br i1/icmp at all:
  - terminated-by-ptr-relaxed-casting.c and region-counter-map.c: predicates (ne/ult/uge/ule/sge) and branch targets are byte-identical; regeneration only added !prof branch-weights (branch_weights 1048575, 1 — trap made
  cold) and !annotation that the stale checks didn't assert. The phi → br → trap: {ubsantrap; unreachable} structure is fully preserved. 
  - flexible-array-member-checks-initialized-O2.c: see below.

  3. Dropped CHECK lines / whole functions — CLEAN. All-prefix function labels: 354 removed / 354 added, identical sets (nothing dropped, including under OPT:/UNOPT:/UNOPT-TF: prefixes). Global CHECK lines: 1288 removed 
  / 1294 added (net +6). Every file is either delta-0 (pure reformat/rename) or net-positive; zero files lost checks.

  The one genuine codegen change (worth a confirming glance)

  In flexible-array-member-checks-initialized-O2.c, function test_under_base_fail, switching to the real Mach-O target changes -O2 output:
  - alloca [20 x i8] and its store go from align 4 → align 1 (natural alignment for the real target).
  - An extra null-check is emitted: icmp eq ptr %bound_ptr_arith, null → br ... %boundscheck.null, %flex.base.nonnull.

  These two are linked: with align 4, LLVM could prove arr-1 ≠ null and folded the null check away; with align 1 it can't, so the runtime check stays. This is safe — a check is added, boundscheck.null is the _or_null
  "skip" path (ends in ret, not a trap), and the trap is still reached via the unchanged FLEX_COUNT_CHECK branch. This file was not regenerated with different tooling (its NOTE line is unchanged), so this reflects real
  arm64-apple-ios codegen.

  Other noteworthy things (not blockers)

  - "NFC" is imprecise. Real IR diffs occur: dso_local dropped throughout (Mach-O linkage), align 4→align 1 on stack/data, and the extra null check above. All are expected consequences of using the correct target — but
  it's more than the "just module flags" the description implies.
  - region-counter-map.c was regenerated with a newer update tool (UTC_ARGS: --version 6, dropping the old --replace-value-regex/--prefix-filecheck-ir-name). It's the only file whose generation args changed. This
  conflates tool-upgrade churn (named [[META]] vars, %[[LABEL]] style, newly-asserted !prof/!annotation, a one-off SSA renumber) with the triple rename, making that file's diff noisy — but the trap/branch structure
  verifies intact.
  - FIXME cleanup: incomplete-array.c / incomplete-array-counted.c drop a // FIXME: Have to use arm64e-apple-iphoneos instead of arm64e-apple-ios to get update_cc_test_checks.py to add IR comment — the workaround this PR
  resolves. (That comment is why the raw arm64e token counts looked unbalanced.) All RUN lines and -verify invocations are preserved with the corrected triple.

  The only thing I'd suggest the author/reviewer sanity-check is that the flexible-array-member-checks-initialized-O2.c output was regenerated against the real compiler (not hand-edited) so the added null-check path is
  genuinely what arm64-apple-ios emits — everything else is mechanically verifiable from the diff.

payload.author: delcypher
payload.body:
Because this PR is so large I had claude look for dropped bounds checks and change to the guards that reach them. It looks ok. This was its summary:

### 1. No traps added or removed
Across the whole diff only **4** `+/-` lines touch `ubsantrap`, and all 4 are pure
FileCheck metadata-index renumbering (`!annotation [[META4]]` → `[[META3]]`) on an
otherwise byte-identical `call void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 25)`. No `ubsantrap` CHECK
line is deleted or introduced anywhere → the set of trap sites is unchanged.

### 2. Branch-condition changes are a single, verified, semantics-preserving fold
Control-flow changes are confined to `-O2` files. The only transformation is
SimplifyCFG collapsing chained short-circuit trap checks into one branch guarded
by an OR built from `select`:
- `br A→trap ; (blk) br B→trap` becomes `OR = select i1 A, i1 true, i1 B; br OR→trap`.
- 3-way chains fold correctly too: `OR2 = select i1 OR, i1 true, i1 C; br OR2→trap`.

Evidence:
- **105 `select` added, 0 removed.** *Every* added select is the poison-safe
  logical-OR idiom `select i1 A, i1 true, i1 B` — 0 AND-folds, 0 data-selects.
- **Per-file invariant holds exactly everywhere:** `(removed br − added br) == added selects`.
  No file removes a trap-guarding branch without a compensating select, so no
  check is silently dropped.
- Trap target label, `!prof` branch weights, and `!annotation` are preserved on
  every folded branch.
- The fold is legal because the second/third guarded load becomes speculatable
  under `dereferenceable(24)` (the pointee is a 24-byte wide-pointer struct).
- `-O0` codegen is unchanged (both bound checks remain as separate branches);
  the only `-O0` line changes are the `META4`→`META3` renumber.

### 3. Signature attribute changes are exactly the intended additions
- 531 added `dereferenceable(N)` are **all `dereferenceable(24)`** — correct and
  uniform for `__bidi_indexable` = `{ptr, upper, lower}` = 24 bytes.
- Only `nofree` + `dereferenceable(24)` are added; **nothing is removed** and no
  other attribute changes appear on signature lines.

### 4. Only-odd-but-benign items (no action required)
- **FileCheck capture renumbering** (`META4`→`META3`, etc.) maps to identical
  annotation *strings* (verified e.g. `!"bounds-safety-check-ptr-ge-lower-bound"`).
- **`__libc_errno` TBAA node drops** out of the aggregate metadata section in
  `soft-traps/call_minimal_custom_func.c`. In the *base* version that node was an
  orphan — defined but never referenced by any function body (the real load uses
  `INT_TBAA1` in both base and head, unchanged). Purely a metadata-listing artifact.
- Minor readability nit: regeneration replaced a couple of descriptive captures
  (e.g. `[[ERRNO_TBAA]]`) with generic `[[META2]]`. Cosmetic churn from
  `update_cc_test_checks.py`; not worth blocking on.

payload.title: Disable tail mem libcalls in swifterror functions

payload.author: hjyamauchi
payload.body:
- **Explanation**:
    A swifterror function whose success path tail-calls into
    memcpy/memmove/memset can miscompile on AArch64/ARM64. The swifterror
    value lives in a fixed physical register (x21) that the function's epilogue
    restores before ret, but SelectionDAG's mem-libcall lowering (and its
    GlobalISel equivalent) computed tail-call eligibility independently of the
    existing SelectionDAGBuilder::LowerCallTo guard that disables tail calls out
    of swifterror functions. So it could still tail-branch straight into the
    libcall, skipping the epilogue and leaving x21 stale. The caller misreads that
    stale value as a nonnull thrown error and crashes dereferencing it. Fix: add a
    hasSwiftErrorArg check and require it at each of these libcall-lowering call
    sites (SelectionDAG and GlobalISel), mirroring the existing guard.

  - **Scope**:
  Narrow. Only affects mem-libcall tail-call eligibility in swifterror
  functions. Ordinary calls already had this guard. No ABI changes.

  - **Issues**:
    https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/issues/90477
    rdar://181625760

  - **Original PRs**:
     https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/214590

  - **Risk**:
    Low. Can only turn an incorrect tail call into a correct ordinary call, never
    the reverse. No runtime/ABI/stdlib changes.

  - **Testing**:
    Added llvm/test/CodeGen/AArch64/swifterror-tailcall-memops.ll, fails before
    this change and passes after. Verified against the original repro from
    swiftlang/swift#90477 (SIGSEGV before, correct after).

  - **Reviewers**: @jroelofs

@AnupamKumar-1 Thank you for all the effort so far, but this PR is getting pretty unwieldy to review. I suggest you split it up into multiple smaller PRs to make it easier to follow. For example:
 - NFC PR migrating from checking ptrattrs to using `isSinglePointerType` et. al.
 - PR adding `AttributedType(Single)` but keeping the ptrattr around and using it for all semantic checks
    - this is probably doable without affecting any tests
 - PR adding the syntax sugar aware helpers, which makes the syntax sugar start having an impact on Sema, but since each case with syntax sugar also has the ptrattr it should be effectively NFC 
 - NFC PR making the utilities private in PointerType
 - PR adding AST printer support for the syntax sugar node
 - PR adding proper type merging support for syntax sugar node
 - PR removing the underlying ptrattr for single
   - can further be split up with separate commits removing it for the implicit and explicit attributes

This way we can start landing changes piecewise.
Keeping the test changes in the same commit as the sema change that caused them will also make it easier to see what affects what, and what doesn't have any effect (or is not tested properly).

payload.body: @ravimad if you can look a little bit into this, or find someone to look into this, it would be great. It affects the Xcode 27 betas, but it is a bug present since at least Xcode 26.2 (probably further, but I have not tested there). It makes the `-define-availability` functionality really broken and can cause unexpected errors depending on the defined availabilities. See swiftlang/swift#90340 for the currently broken behaviour that this change would fix.

payload.author: tshortli
payload.body: This is a welcome fix in general and it should be taken for Swift `main`. However, I don't think the reward is strong enough to justify inclusion in Swift 6.4 at this point in the release. `-define-availability` is not an official feature of Swift, and working around the issues that this bug causes for users of `-define-availability` is trivial once the problem is identified. The impact of suddenly breaking `-define-availability` source compatibility, or subtly changing some other behavior that depends on VersionTuple hashing, would be very high this late in the release.

payload.author: drodriguez
payload.body:
> This is a welcome fix in general and it should be taken for Swift `main`. However, I don't think the reward is strong enough to justify inclusion in Swift 6.4 at this point in the release. `-define-availability` is not an official feature of Swift, 

`-define-availability` is part of the output of `--help` of both the driver and the frontend in `swiftc`:

https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/44711f85d89c14eb3ec81d5e1e2a23395fccee39/include/swift/Option/Options.td#L584-L587

Not sure if "official" is another level that needs to be in a different surface, but you don't even need `--help-hidden` to learn about it.

> and working around the issues that this bug causes for users of `-define-availability` is trivial once the problem is identified.

I respectfully disagree with this being trivial or possible to work around. It is because we could not work around these issues in a nice, future-proof way that we had to find the root cause and try to fix it.

We have a set of macros that help us to not forget any platform and deal with version number differences before the Apple homogeneization, so we only write `if #available(SDKLevel 26, *)` instead of the more error-prone `if #available(macOS 26, iOS 26, …)` (people were forgetting platforms all the time).  We had to define both `X` and `X.0` because we find out that writing `if #available(Foo X)` or `if #available(Foo X.0)` was not working when only one of them was defined. That started breaking with the introduction of the beta SDKs for 27.0, when we added new values for the 27.0 equivalents, suddenly `SDKLevel 16.0` started being reported as duplicated of `SDKLevel 16`, but the same was not happening for 14, 15, 17, 18, 26. If we removed the `X.0`, then we started having problems in some of those 14, 15, 17, 18, 26 because people were using both `X` and `X.0` in the source code. We can try to change them all, and try to explain to people that you need to be precise and use the exact one… but not for 16, because that one is special. Or we can try to keep a list of ones that do not need to be duplicated, but this only appeared with our introduction of 27 might mean that "tomorrow" with 27.1 a new bucket layout is needed and 16 might need 16.0 or another one might need to remove its duplicate.

> The impact of suddenly breaking `-define-availability` source compatibility

I don't agree that this is breaking "source compatibility", because the system is coded in a way that both `X` and `X.0` should have been considered the same version (there's a compiler error for the cases of duplicated defined availabilities already), so this was already broken, and someone relying on defining both `X` and `X.0` was not doing it expecting to work, but because of this bug it was impossible to match both `X.0` and `X` when defining only one. The current behaviour is already "breaking" since suddenly defining a new availability level breaks a compilation that was working before, and not in the new version, but a version that has been working for years.

> or subtly changing some other behavior that depends on VersionTuple hashing, would be very high this late in the release.

As I wrote in the initial summary, I found other usages of `DenseMapInfo<VersionTuple>`, and I don't disagree that it might change behaviour in some way. As I said, the current test suite does not seem to surface any significant behavioural change, and in our internal testing (quite large codebase), we have not observed anything derived from this, but I cannot ensure you there is nothing. It definitely should change, but, in my opinion, for the better, if anything.

Your codebase, your releases. Hope you can consider this for a 6.4.1 or similar instead of waiting until Spring 2027 release to get this.

payload.author: drodriguez
payload.body:
Just found out swiftlang/swift#90958 which makes `-define-availability` not longer appear in `--help` and relegates it to `--help-hidden`. I would had preferred other solutions, instead of trying to "get the cat back into the bag" (like merging this).

It would be nice to at least have an answer to my last question in the previous comment: can we consider this for a 6.4.1 or similar instead of waiting until the Spring 2027 release to get this bug fixed? Since I don't have visibility into your internal processes, I imagine I can ping this thread at some moment in September, but it would be nice to know if that would even work before setting a reminder.

payload.author: tshortli
payload.body:
There were a number of flags, including `-define-availability`, that should never have been exposed as `swiftc` flags for general users. My intention wasn't to "resolve" this issue by hiding the flag. The flag's exposure is a problem on its own because `-define-availability` is not a feature of the compiler that has been intentionally made public; it hasn't gone through Swift Evolution and isn't suitable for general consumption.

That doesn't mean we shouldn't fix this bug, of course, but it's just way too late in the 6.4 release process to take this particular fix. I think taking it in a dot release of 6.4 could make sense if you want to renominate the fix once branches for that have been announced.

payload.author: delcypher
payload.body:
@hnrklssn 

> Surely this is also a problem at desk and not just in CI? Which is why I'm asking if we can't just copy what LLDB is doing.

This problem doesn't exist for LLDB testing because they don't try to use a system LLDB. Instead they are building LLDB from source. That creates a whole set of other problems but there isn't a python version mismatch problem in that scenario because the bindings are generated for the python version that CMake was configured with. So the python versions are **always** in sync by construction.

Our scenario is different because we are supporting

* Using the LLDB shipped in Xcode. The advantage of supporting this is you don't need to build a working LLDB to run the `-fbounds-safety` runtime tests. This means less work in CI and less work at desk. To make this work though you need have use a python version that matches what the LLDB bindings inside Xcode were built with. This patch makes this work out the box instead of requiring the developer to know how to precisely configure things.
* Using a locally built LLDB. The advantage of supporting this is we get to use the latest stuff in LLDB and it avoids the hacks I had to put in to workaround the fact the "LLDB shipped in Xcode" on the CI nodes is old and out of sync with the clang being tested.

Ideally I'd like to move to using the just-built LLDB in CI but doing that requires that we solve some other problems first.

A few notes:

1. This dependency should be enabled by LLVM_INCLUDE_TESTS as this is a test-only dependency. You can check the code a few lines above the CMake change to see how to check for that.

2. Also, the dependency should only be activated if bounds-safety is in COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES

I'm also not sure if this is the right approach. With this change, there is now a dependency from compiler-rt on LLDB, but check-lldb now also has a dependency on compiler-rt as we tests bounds-safety. So every change in `lldb/*` now retriggers the compiler-rt build, which is very tedious.

payload.author: delcypher
payload.body:
@Teemperor Thanks for catching these issues.


> A few notes:
> 
> 1. This dependency should be enabled by LLVM_INCLUDE_TESTS as this is a test-only dependency. You can check the code a few lines above the CMake change to see how to check for that.

Thanks for spotting that. I'll put up a patch to fix that (rdar://184144696).

> 2. Also, the dependency should only be activated if bounds-safety is in COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES

I've filed rdar://184145099 to track whatever we do here. Fixing that is a little tricky. `COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES` is CMake cache variable of the compiler-rt build which is a sub-build (`ExternalProject` in CMake terminology). The parent build where this CMake code runs doesn't know what `COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES` is going to be set to by the sub-build unless the value is explicitly provided to the parent build by the user (so it's value can be propagated into the the sub-build).

The only good short-term way I can think of fixing that is moving the definition of `COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES` into a common file that the parent build and sub-build can **both** include and the sub-build can include. This way the definition of the default value and its documentation isn't duplicated. If we do that then we can query the value of `COMPILER_RT_ENABLE_TEST_SUITES` in the parent build to avoid adding the dependency when the `-fbounds-safety` tests are off.

Technically the dependency also depends on `COMPILER_RT_BOUNDS_SAFETY_USE_JUST_BUILT_LLDB` so it could guard on this too. Pulling variables out of the sub-build though is a little messy and it's something I'd like to avoid doing a lot of unless we can help it.

> I'm also not sure if this is the right approach. With this change, there is now a dependency from compiler-rt on LLDB, but check-lldb now also has a dependency on compiler-rt as we tests bounds-safety. So every change in lldb/* now retriggers the compiler-rt build, which is very tedious.

So the dependency is there because picking which LLDB to use for testing in compiler-rt is a configuration time decision. The dependency was put there to ensure the lldb binary and python bindings get built before we try to configure compiler-rt and build it.

> So every change in lldb/* now retriggers the compiler-rt build, which is very tedious.

Yeah that's not great. That will definitely trigger a reconfigure of compiler-rt, but after that happens is the build quick (i.e. does it skip rebuilding the libraries because clang and the sources didn't change?).

A more longer term way to avoid this is to have a new sub-project in `llvm-project` that is dedicated to doing runtime testing using the just built Clang. Then move the `-fbounds-safety` tests there. This sub-project wouldn't have any build time components so the worse that'll happen is a reconfigure (which should be pretty fast compared to compiler-rt) of the sub-project would happen when you change LLDB (if you have the sub-project enabled).

A short term solution here could be just to remove adding the dependency. CI doesn't currently use this build mode. It's mostly here for my at desk development.
